The curriculum

Six modules, in order. Each one ends in something that runs.

Module 01 · Foundations

What a mod actually is

Before you open a single file, get the mental model straight: how a Quest game loads its code, where a mod can insert itself, and why that choice decides everything else you do.

mod loaderil2cpp vs monopatch vs loadread · 25 min

Two ways to change a game

Every mod you will ever write falls into one of two families, and almost every beginner mistake comes from confusing them.

Patching means editing the game's files on disk. You change a byte in a library, a number in a config, a texture in a bundle — then you repackage the app and install it. The change is permanent, it lives in the build, and it is there before the game even starts.

Loading means leaving the game's files alone and injecting your own code at runtime. A mod loader gets itself started early, then hooks the functions you care about while the game is running. Nothing on disk changes except the loader itself.

ApproachChangesGood forCost
PatchingBytes in the APKConstants, assets, text, textures, simple value tweaksRe-sign and re-install for every change
LoadingNothing — code injected at runtimeNew behaviour, menus, toggles, anything you want on/off liveNeeds a loader that works on your target

This course teaches patching first, because it is concrete and you can see the result immediately. Module 5 then brings in a loader so your mods can have an actual menu.

What a Quest game is, physically

A Quest headset runs Android. A Quest game is therefore an APK — and an APK is a ZIP file with a strict layout and a signature. Rename one to .zip and your file manager will happily open it.

The overwhelming majority of Quest games are built in Unity, compiled with IL2CPP. That one fact shapes everything:

  • The developer wrote C#.
  • Unity converted that C# into C++, then compiled it to native ARM64 machine code.
  • The result is one big shared library: lib/arm64-v8a/libil2cpp.so.
  • The art, audio, scenes and prefabs live separately in assets/bin/Data/ — mostly inside data.unity3d and .resource files.
Why this matters

Because the C# was compiled to native code, you cannot open a Quest Unity game in a C# decompiler and read tidy method bodies the way you can with a PC Mono build. You are reading ARM64. That is the single biggest difference between PC modding and Quest modding, and it is why the toolchain looks the way it does.

Managed, native, and why the difference bites

Managed code runs on a virtual machine. On Android that is Java/Kotlin compiled to DEX bytecode and executed by ART. DEX is structured and self-describing — class names, method names and types are all still in the file, which makes it comparatively pleasant to read and edit.

Native code is machine instructions the CPU runs directly. ARM64 in a .so file. There are no method names unless the developer left symbols in, no types, and no safety net. It is just instructions and addresses.

In a typical Quest game you will find both:

Lives inFormatUsually holds
classes.dexDEX bytecode (managed)The Android wrapper — activity, permissions, SDK glue, platform calls
libil2cpp.soARM64 (native)The entire game: your gameplay logic, physics tuning, scoring, everything the developer wrote in C#
libunity.soARM64 (native)The Unity engine itself — you rarely touch this
data.unity3dUnity bundleScenes, meshes, textures, audio, prefabs

Rule of thumb: if it is gameplay, it is in libil2cpp.so. If it is Android plumbing, it is in classes.dex. If it is something you can see or hear, it is in the bundles.

The loop you will repeat forever

Every mod, from a one-byte tweak to a full menu, goes around the same six-step loop. Learn it now and the rest of the course is just filling in detail.

the modding loop
1. OPEN     load a copy of the APK in Teardown Bench
2. FIND     search strings / symbols / values for your target
3. READ     disassemble around the hit, confirm it is the right thing
4. CHANGE   patch the bytes, staged as a reversible patch set
5. BUILD    rebuild, zipalign, sign with your own key
6. TEST     adb install, put the headset on, see if it worked
           ↺ it did not work the first time. go to 2.

Step 6 failing is not a setback, it is the job. Most of the skill in modding is narrowing down which of steps 2–4 was wrong, quickly.

Your toolchain

  • Teardown Bench — open, search, disassemble, patch, extract assets, rebuild and sign. It is mounted in this page; press B or hit "Open bench" any time.
  • Mod Studio — scans a build, works out what is moddable, and assembles the menu. Module 5.
  • adb — Android Debug Bridge, from Google's platform-tools. How you talk to the headset. Module 6.
  • A keystore — your own signing key. You generate it once and reuse it forever. Module 6.
Work on a copy

Always keep one untouched original APK somewhere you will not overwrite. The bench tracks edits as reversible patch sets, but a pristine backup is still the fastest route back to a known-good state when an experiment goes sideways.

Scope of this course

Everything here is aimed at games and builds you own and are permitted to modify — your own projects, offline and single-player tinkering, on your own headset. Modding other people's live or multiplayer games, or anything that touches other players, is out of scope and not covered.

Knowledge check

Did it land?

Three questions. Pick an answer to see why.

A Quest Unity game's gameplay logic — the C# the developer actually wrote — ends up where?

libil2cpp.so. IL2CPP converts the C# to C++ and compiles it to native ARM64. That is why you read disassembly rather than decompiled C# on Quest.

You want a mod the player can toggle on and off while playing. Which family?

Loading. A patched byte is baked in before launch, so it cannot be toggled. Anything the player switches at runtime needs code running inside the process — a loader and a hook.

An APK is, structurally speaking…

A ZIP. That is exactly why the bench can open it, list entries, and rebuild it — and why the signature has to be reapplied after you change anything.

Module 02 · Read the game

Opening a build and finding your way

Load a real APK in the bench and learn its anatomy — what each file is for, how to search gigabytes without melting the tab, and how to turn a vague idea into an exact offset.

AndroidManifestfile treestreaming searchhands-on

Load it

Open the bench (B), then either drag an APK onto the window or use Open folder if you have an extracted build. The bench parses the ZIP central directory, lists every entry, and never inflates anything it does not need to — which is how a 184 MB game opens in a couple of seconds instead of eating a gigabyte of memory.

Once loaded you get the file tree on the left, a tabbed viewer in the middle, and the search/changes dock below. That is the whole instrument.

The anatomy of a Quest APK

Here is what you are looking at, top to bottom.

PathWhat it isTouch it?
AndroidManifest.xmlBinary XML. Package name, version, permissions, activities, VR flags.Sometimes — e.g. to read the package name
classes.dexManaged Android code. May be several: classes2.dex and so on.For platform/plumbing changes
lib/arm64-v8a/libil2cpp.soThe compiled game. Usually the biggest native file.Yes — this is where gameplay lives
lib/arm64-v8a/libunity.soThe Unity engine runtime.Rarely
assets/bin/Data/data.unity3dThe main Unity bundle — scenes, meshes, textures, audio.Swap whole bundles; see the note below
assets/bin/Data/Managed/Metadata/global-metadata.datIL2CPP metadata: the string literals, type and method names the runtime still needs.Read it constantly — it is your map
META-INF/The existing signature. Invalidated the moment you change anything.No — it gets replaced on re-sign
resources.arscCompiled resources: strings, layouts, app name.For cosmetic/label changes
global-metadata.dat is the Rosetta stone

IL2CPP strips names from the compiled code but the runtime still needs them for reflection and strings, so they survive here. When you search for a method or a literal and get a hit in this file, you have found the name — the next job is finding the native code that uses it.

Searching a build that is bigger than memory

The two files you most want to search — libil2cpp.so and data.unity3d — are also the two biggest. Naive tools skip them. The bench streams them in 4 MiB windows with carry-over between windows, so a match that straddles a window boundary is still found and every offset reported is absolute and exact.

Three search modes you will use constantly:

  • Text — a UTF-8 or UTF-16 string. Best first move: search for words you see in-game. Menu labels, achievement names, error text.
  • Hex — raw byte sequences. For instruction patterns and known constants.
  • Value — a typed number. Floats are the big one; module 4 covers why.

From "I want to change X" to an offset

This is the actual skill. Work backwards from something visible.

worked example — finding a gameplay constant
# 1. something you can see in-game
search text   "Sprint"
  → global-metadata.dat @ 0x1a4f20     a method or field name

# 2. is there a matching symbol?
symbols       sprint
  → set_sprintSpeed   libil2cpp.so @ 0x00c41a80
  → get_sprintSpeed   libil2cpp.so @ 0x00c41a60

# 3. read the code around it
disasm        0x00c41a60
  → ldr  s0, [x0, #0x4c]              reads a float field
  → ret

# 4. now you know the field offset: +0x4c on the player object

Not every game leaves symbols in. When yours does not, the path is longer: find the string in metadata, find the metadata index, then find the code that loads that index. The bench's symbol resolver automates most of that — but understanding the chain is what lets you recover when it does not.

Pin as you go

Every interesting offset you find, pin it. You will lose it otherwise, and re-deriving an address you already found is the single biggest time sink in this hobby. Pins persist with the loaded build and travel with your patch sets.

Knowledge check

Did it land?

Two questions on navigating a build.

You search for the word "Sprint" and the only hit is in global-metadata.dat. What have you found?

The name. Metadata holds the strings and identifiers IL2CPP kept for the runtime. Finding the name is step one; locating the native code that uses it is step two.

Why does the bench stream large files in windows with carry-over instead of reading them whole?

Memory, plus correctness at the seams. A 180 MB library read whole would blow the tab's heap. Carry-over between windows is what keeps a match that straddles the boundary from being missed.

Module 03 · Native & managed code

Reading ARM64 and DEX

Just enough assembly to recognise what a function does, spot its return value, and know the difference between an edit that sticks and one that quietly does nothing.

AArch64DEX bytecodecalling conventionread · 40 min

You do not need to learn ARM64. You need to recognise six things.

Nobody reads assembly fluently at the start, and you do not have to. Modding needs pattern recognition, not fluency. Here is essentially the whole working vocabulary.

ThingLooks likeMeans
Registersx0–x30 / w0–w3064-bit / 32-bit general purpose. x0 is argument one and the return value.
Float registerss0–s31 / d0–d3132-bit float / 64-bit double. s0 returns a float.
Loadldr w0, [x8, #0x20]Read memory at x8+0x20 into w0. Reading a field.
Storestr w1, [x8, #0x20]Write w1 into memory. Writing a field.
Movemov w0, #1Put a constant into a register.
ReturnretReturn to caller. Whatever is in x0/w0/s0 is the result.

That is it. Branches (b, bl, cbz, b.eq) fill in the gaps, and you will pick those up by reading.

The shape of a getter

IL2CPP compiles C# properties into tiny, extremely recognisable functions. Learn this shape and you can identify hundreds of functions at a glance.

get_maxHealth() — a float property getter
; C#:  public float maxHealth { get { return _maxHealth; } }
0x00c41a60  ldr   s0, [x0, #0x4c]   ; load float at this+0x4c into s0
0x00c41a64  ret                     ; return it

Two instructions. x0 on entry is this — the object. #0x4c is the field's offset inside that object. s0 carries the float back out. Once you have seen one, you have seen them all.

A setter is the mirror image:

set_maxHealth(float)
0x00c41a80  str   s0, [x0, #0x4c]   ; store the argument into this+0x4c
0x00c41a84  ret

The shape of a bool

Methods that answer a yes/no question compile to something equally tidy, and this is the pattern you will meet most often when a feature is gated behind a flag.

a boolean-returning method
; returns true
mov   w0, #1
ret

; returns false
mov   w0, #0
ret

; reads a stored flag and returns it
ldrb  w0, [x0, #0x31]
ret

Which is why "stub it to return a constant" is such a common move: a boolean method is often literally two instructions, and replacing them with mov w0,#1 ; ret is an eight-byte edit. For your own builds — a debug flag you want forced on, a tutorial gate you want skipped — this is the whole technique.

DEX, by contrast, is readable

The managed side keeps its names, so classes.dex disassembles into something close to legible.

DEX bytecode — a boolean method
.method public isTutorialComplete()Z
    .registers 2
    iget-boolean  v0, p0, Lcom/game/Save;->tutorialDone:Z
    return        v0
.end method

Note what survives: the class path, the field name, the type signature (Z is boolean). Editing DEX is friendlier than editing native code — but remember, on a Unity Quest game there is usually very little gameplay here.

Edits that stick vs edits that do nothing

This is the lesson that saves you the most wasted evenings.

  • Editing a string in metadata changes what is displayed. It does not change behaviour. Renaming a method's string does not reroute any call.
  • Editing a constant in code changes behaviour — if you found the right constant and it is not recomputed somewhere else.
  • Editing a field's default only matters if nothing overwrites it at runtime. Unity serialises most tuning values into the scene, so a default in code is frequently ignored.
The Unity serialisation trap

You patch a float in libil2cpp.so, rebuild, install — and nothing changes. Nine times out of ten the value is also stored in the scene inside data.unity3d, and Unity overwrites your patched default when the object is deserialised. If a code patch has no effect, suspect the bundle next.

Byte-length discipline

ARM64 instructions are all exactly 4 bytes. That gives you one hard rule: a patch must be the same length as what it replaces. You can swap two instructions for two other instructions. You cannot insert a third without relocating everything after it, which is a different and much harder job.

When you need more room than you have, that is the signal to stop patching and start loading — a hook gives you unlimited space because your code lives elsewhere. That is module 5.

Knowledge check

Did it land?

Three on reading code.

In ldr s0, [x0, #0x4c] followed by ret, what is 0x4c?

A field offset. x0 is this; [x0, #0x4c] is the field sitting 0x4c bytes into the object. The value loaded from there goes back in s0.

You patched a float in libil2cpp.so, rebuilt and installed — no change in game. Most likely cause?

Unity serialisation. Tuning values set in the editor live in the scene data, not the code default. When a code patch has no visible effect, the bundle is the next place to look.

Why can't you insert an extra instruction into the middle of an ARM64 function?

It shifts everything after it. Instructions are fixed-width and addresses are baked in, so a patch has to be length-preserving. When you need more room, hook at runtime instead.

Module 04 · Your first gameplay mod

Change one number, feel it in VR

The full loop end to end on something small: find a value, understand its bytes, patch it as a reversible change, and verify you hit the right thing before you ever build.

float searchIEEE-754patch setsbuild one

Pick something you can feel

For a first mod, choose a value with an obvious, immediate physical effect. Jump height. Movement speed. Grab distance. Throw force. You want something you will notice within three seconds of putting the headset on — because the whole point of the first one is a fast, unambiguous feedback loop.

Bad first targets: anything cosmetic (you will not be sure it worked), anything on a timer (slow to test), anything that only matters after ten minutes of play.

Floats, and why searching for "4.5" fails

Game tuning values are nearly always 32-bit floats, and a float is not stored as text. 4.5 lives in the file as four bytes in IEEE-754 form. Search for the characters "4.5" and you will find documentation and nothing else.

how a float actually sits in the file
  value        bytes (little-endian)     search as
  1.0          00 00 80 3F               hex
  2.0          00 00 00 40               hex
  4.5          00 00 90 40               hex
  9.0          00 00 10 41               hex
  100.0        00 00 C8 42               hex

# the bench's value search does this conversion for you —
# type 4.5, pick f32, and it searches the right bytes.
Round numbers are your friend

Values like 1.0, 2.0 and 0.5 appear thousands of times in a build — too many hits to be useful. An odd value like 4.37 or 12.5 appears once or twice. When a game exposes an unusual tuning number, that is the easiest thing in the world to find.

Narrowing the hits

A float search will give you more hits than you want. Narrow them like this:

  1. File first. Hits in libil2cpp.so are code or constants. Hits in data.unity3d are serialised scene values. Decide which one you are after — and remember from module 3 that the scene usually wins.
  2. Neighbourhood. Tuning values cluster. If you find your jump height sitting next to three other plausible movement floats, you are almost certainly in the right struct.
  3. Symbols. If the build kept symbols, search the symbol list for the concept first and let that point you at the offset, rather than searching the value blind.
  4. Change one, test. When two candidates look equally good, patch one, build, test. Ambiguity resolved in one cycle.

Make the edit reversible

Use the value tweaker rather than typing raw hex. You give it the offset, the type and the new value; it writes the correct bytes and records the change in a patch set — an ordered, named, reversible list of every edit you have staged.

a staged patch set
patch set "higher jump"
  [1] libil2cpp.so 0x00c41a60  f32  4.5 → 9.0
  [2] libil2cpp.so 0x00c41b14  f32  1.0 → 1.4   air control

  revert [1]        undo one edit
  revert all       back to the original build
  export            save the set and re-apply to a future version

That last one matters more than it looks. When the game updates, your offsets move — but an exported patch set is a written record of exactly what you changed and why, which turns re-doing the work from an archaeology project into a half-hour.

Verify before you build

Building and installing takes minutes. Checking takes seconds. Before every build:

  • Re-read the bytes at the offset. Confirm they are what you intended to write.
  • Check the length. A 4-byte float replaced 4 bytes. Nothing shifted.
  • Disassemble around it. If you patched inside code rather than a constant pool, make sure you did not land in the middle of an instruction.
  • Sanity-check the value. Setting jump force to 9000 does not give you a fun mod, it gives you a player who clips through the ceiling and falls forever. Start with roughly double.
Change one thing per build

Stage one edit, build, test. If you change five values at once and the game crashes on launch, you have learned nothing except that one of five things is wrong. The discipline feels slow and is dramatically faster.

Your assignment

Before moving on: pick one value in a build you own, find it, patch it, and get it running on your headset with a visible difference. Module 6 covers the build-and-install half if you want to read ahead — but do not skip actually doing it. Everything after this assumes you have been round the loop once.

Knowledge check

Did it land?

Two on making the change.

Searching the text "4.5" to find a jump-height float returns nothing useful. Why?

It's binary, not text. Search by typed value (f32) and let the tool convert, or search the hex bytes directly.

Why stage edits as a patch set rather than writing bytes directly?

Reversibility and portability. You can undo one edit without rebuilding from scratch, and when offsets move in the next version the exported set tells you exactly what you changed and why.

Module 05 · Design the menu

Build a mod menu in Mod Studio

Patching one value is a mod. A menu is a product — toggles the player flips in the headset. Let the studio read your build, tell it what you want, and watch the panel assemble in front of you.

Mod Studiocapability scanmenu.jsondesign it

Why a menu changes everything

A patched constant is fixed at build time. A menu means your mod has state: the player turns things on and off, adjusts values, sees what is active. That requires code running inside the game, which is why this module is where loading finally replaces patching.

The practical upshot is that you stop shipping five different APKs for five different tweaks and start shipping one build with five toggles.

Let it read the build first

Open Mod Studio (press M) and drop your APK on the scanner. It parses the archive, reads the native image and the il2cpp metadata, and indexes every symbol it finds in there.

What comes back is a list of systems it recognised, each with a confidence score and the evidence behind it — how many references it saw and which names they were. That list is not decoration: a control the studio can point at a real field will work, and one it cannot is a control you will have to wire yourself.

  • Panel — what the player sees floating in front of them. Title, credit, and the controls stacked down it.
  • Controls — toggles, sliders and buttons, each bound to a field in the build.
  • Evidence — the symbol each control is wired to, carried through into the export.
Design for arms, not for mice

A menu that looks tidy on a monitor is often miserable in VR. Buttons need to be big — a comfortable target is far larger than you think. Keep the panel within easy reach, below eye line, and never put anything important at the edges where the player has to turn their head.

Just say what you want

Type it in plain English. "Let me fly and double my speed." "Low gravity." "Make me invincible." The studio maps the request onto what it found in your build and adds the controls, telling you which symbols it bound each one to.

If you ask for something it has no recipe for, it does not give up — it searches the symbols it indexed from your build for the closest match and derives a control from that. Ask for "wall jump charges" and it will go looking for anything in your game that resembles it.

a toggle button's blocks
when [ Super Jump ] toggled
  if <toggle is on>
      set player.jumpForce to 9.0
      show toast "Super jump ON"
  else
      set player.jumpForce to 4.5    ; the original
      show toast "Super jump OFF"

Note the else branch. The commonest beginner bug in a mod menu is a toggle that turns something on and cannot turn it off, because the original value was never stored. Always capture the starting value and restore it.

The preview is live

The panel on the right is the real thing, not a picture of it. Flip a toggle and it flips. Drag a slider and the value moves. Rename the menu and the header changes. Move your cursor across it and it tilts, so you can see how it will read at an angle in the headset.

Checking a layout here takes seconds. Checking the same layout after a rebuild, re-sign, install and headset-on takes about ten minutes. Over an evening that difference is the whole evening.

Export and close the loop

Export gives you three things:

  • menu.json — the layout and the binding for every control, as data.
  • libTEAR.cpp — the same menu as a source scaffold, if you would rather hand-edit it or compile it into the loader yourself.
  • loader.cfg — what the loader reads at startup, including the hotkey that opens the panel.

Back in the bench: Mod menu → Import menu. The menu is written into the APK as two new files, and the loader reads them at startup.

what import adds to the build
  + assets/teardown/menu.json    your layout + block logic
  + assets/teardown/loader.cfg   tells the loader to read it at startup

  the other 78 entries are copied across untouched —
  only the two new files get compressed.

Build the APK as normal and the menu rides along inside it. That is the full loop: designed on the bench, tested on the bench, shipped in the build.

Knowledge check

Did it land?

Two on menus.

Why does a mod menu require loading rather than patching?

Runtime state. A patched byte is fixed before launch. Toggling something while playing means your code has to be alive in the process — that's a loader and a hook.

Your toggle turns Super Jump on but can never turn it off. Most likely cause?

No stored original. Capture the starting value when the toggle first fires, and restore it in the else branch — otherwise "off" has no value to go back to.

Module 06 · Ship it

Rebuild, sign, sideload

The last mile, and the one that trips up most beginners. Rebuild without bloating the APK, align it, sign it with your own key, and get it onto the headset — plus how to read the error when it refuses.

zipalignapksigneradb installdeploy

Rebuild

Hit Rebuild in the bench. Files you did not edit are copied out of the source APK still compressed — original CRC, original compression method, byte for byte. Only what you actually changed is recompressed.

That matters more than it sounds. A naive writer that inflates everything turns a 184 MB game into a ~280 MB output and needs about a gigabyte of memory to do it — which simply crashes the tab. Copying untouched entries through keeps the rebuild at a couple of seconds and the output the same size as the input.

It comes out as .zip

The rebuilt file downloads with a .zip extension. Rename it to .apk before doing anything else — the tools below will not touch it otherwise.

Make a keystore — once, forever

Android will not install an unsigned APK. You need a signing key; you generate it one time and reuse it for everything you ever build.

generate your signing key (do this once)
keytool -genkey -v \
  -keystore my-release.keystore \
  -alias questforge \
  -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000
Keep it and keep the password

Back the keystore up somewhere you will still have it in a year. Android treats an update signed with a different key as a different app — so losing it means every future build has to be uninstalled-then-installed rather than updated in place, and any saved data goes with it.

Align, then sign — in that order

Order is not optional. zipalign rewrites offsets; signing after alignment is fine, aligning after signing breaks the signature.

align and sign
# 1. align — uncompressed entries land on 4-byte boundaries
zipalign -p -f 4 rebuilt.apk aligned.apk

# 2. sign with your key
apksigner sign \
  --ks my-release.keystore \
  --ks-key-alias questforge \
  --out final.apk \
  aligned.apk

# 3. confirm it took
apksigner verify --print-certs final.apk

Both tools ship in Android's build-tools; adb is in platform-tools. Put both on your PATH and this becomes muscle memory.

Onto the headset

Enable developer mode on the headset, plug it in, accept the USB debugging prompt while wearing it (the dialog appears in VR and people miss it constantly), then:

install and watch
adb devices                      # confirm the headset is listed
adb install -r final.apk         # -r replaces an existing install

# if -r is refused, the signature differs from what's installed:
adb uninstall com.yourgame.package
adb install final.apk

# watch it start (Unity logs here)
adb logcat -s Unity

When it refuses — reading the error

ErrorMeansFix
INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLEInstalled copy was signed with a different keyUninstall first, then install
INSTALL_PARSE_FAILED_NO_CERTIFICATESNot signed, or signing failed silentlyRe-run apksigner; verify with --print-certs
INSTALL_FAILED_INVALID_APKAlignment or archive structure is wrongRe-run zipalign before signing
INSTALL_FAILED_INSUFFICIENT_STORAGEHeadset is fullFree space; VR builds are large
Installs, then crashes instantlyYour patch broke somethingRevert the patch set, confirm clean build runs, re-apply one edit at a time
Always prove the clean build installs

Before blaming your patch, rebuild and sign the unmodified APK and install that. If the clean build also fails, the problem is in your build and signing steps, not your edit — and you have just saved yourself an hour of looking in the wrong place.

You've done it

That is the complete loop: open, find, read, change, build, test. Everything beyond this point is the same six steps applied to harder targets — and the bench, the menu designer and the reference are all here whenever you need them.

Knowledge check

Did it land?

Three on shipping.

Correct order for the last two steps?

Align first. zipalign rewrites entry offsets, which would invalidate a signature applied before it.

INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE means…

Signature mismatch. Android only updates in place when the signing key matches. Uninstall, then install fresh.

Your modded build crashes on launch. Best first move?

Bisect it. Prove the clean build runs first — that separates a broken build process from a broken patch, which are completely different problems.

Everything you'll reach for mid-build. Click any block to copy it.

adb — talking to the headset

adb ships in Android platform-tools. Enable developer mode on the headset, plug in over USB, and accept the debugging prompt while wearing it.

everyday adb
adb devices                               # list attached devices
adb install -r final.apk                  # install, replacing existing
adb uninstall com.pkg.name               # remove it
adb shell pm list packages | grep game     # find a package name
adb shell pm path com.pkg.name           # where the APK lives on device
adb pull /data/app/.../base.apk          # pull a build off the headset
adb logcat -s Unity                       # watch Unity logs only
adb logcat *:E                            # errors only
adb shell am start -n com.pkg/.MainActivity  # launch it
adb shell dumpsys package com.pkg | grep versionName

Building and signing

keystore · align · sign · verify
# once: make your signing key
keytool -genkey -v -keystore my-release.keystore \
  -alias questforge -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000

# every build: align BEFORE signing
zipalign -p -f 4 rebuilt.apk aligned.apk

apksigner sign --ks my-release.keystore \
  --ks-key-alias questforge --out final.apk aligned.apk

apksigner verify --print-certs final.apk

APK anatomy at a glance

PathWhat it holdsWhere gameplay hides
AndroidManifest.xmlBinary XML — package, version, permissionsNo
classes.dexManaged Android code (DEX)Platform glue only
lib/arm64-v8a/libil2cpp.soThe compiled C# — native ARM64Yes — primary target
lib/arm64-v8a/libunity.soUnity engine runtimeRarely
assets/bin/Data/data.unity3dScenes, meshes, textures, audioSerialised tuning values
…/Metadata/global-metadata.datIL2CPP names and string literalsYour map to the code
resources.arscCompiled resources, app labelNo
META-INF/Signature — replaced on re-signNo

ARM64 cheat sheet

InstructionDoes
ldr w0, [x8, #0x20]Load 32-bit value from x8+0x20 into w0 — reading a field
ldr s0, [x0, #0x4c]Load a float into s0 — reading a float field
ldrb w0, [x0, #0x31]Load a single byte — reading a bool
str w1, [x8, #0x20]Store w1 into memory — writing a field
mov w0, #1Put constant 1 into w0 — "return true"
retReturn; x0 / w0 / s0 carries the result
bl 0x…Call a function
cbz w0, 0x…Branch if w0 is zero

Every ARM64 instruction is exactly 4 bytes. Patches must preserve length.

Float bytes

common f32 values, little-endian
  0.5  00 00 00 3F      10.0  00 00 20 41
  1.0  00 00 80 3F      50.0  00 00 48 42
  2.0  00 00 00 40     100.0  00 00 C8 42
  4.5  00 00 90 40    1000.0  00 00 7A 44
  9.0  00 00 10 41       0.0  00 00 00 00

Glossary

APKAndroid application package. A ZIP with a required layout and a signature. A Quest game is one.
IL2CPPUnity's pipeline that converts C# to C++ and compiles it to native code. Why you read ARM64 on Quest.
global-metadata.datThe names and string literals IL2CPP kept for the runtime. Your map from a word you saw in-game to the code behind it.
DEXDalvik Executable — managed Android bytecode in classes.dex. Keeps names and types, so it reads far more easily than native code.
ARM64 / AArch64The 64-bit ARM instruction set the Quest CPU runs. Fixed 4-byte instructions.
Mod loaderCode that starts early inside the game process and loads your mods at runtime, instead of editing files on disk.
HookRedirecting an existing function to your code so you can change behaviour without rewriting the original.
Patch setAn ordered, named, reversible list of staged edits — individually undoable and exportable to re-apply after an update.
zipalignAligns uncompressed entries to 4-byte boundaries so Android can memory-map them. Run before signing.
apksignerGoogle's signing tool. Applies the v2+ signature scheme Android requires to install.
SideloadInstalling an APK directly over adb rather than through a store.
Unity bundledata.unity3d and friends — scenes, meshes, textures, audio, and the serialised values that often override code defaults.

Need something that isn't here? Open the bench — the tools dock has the full symbol list, hex view and manifest reader for whatever build you have loaded.

Mod Studio · on-device

Scan a build. Say what you want. Watch the menu appear.

The engine runs on your own machine. It reads the build you load, indexes every symbol inside it, and works out what is moddable. Ask for anything — if it has no recipe for what you want, it derives one from the symbols it found in your game. No account, no upload, no network call.

Scannersample build
Drop an APK here or browse — parsed on this machine, nothing uploads built libTEAR.so goes here too

MOD MENU @yourhandle
v1.0 · build 240● LIVE

The dot is the pointer you get in the headset \u2014 it floats off your wrist. It is drawn by the runtime, not baked into the panel.

How to make it work nothing to wire

In the bench: Mod menu → Import menu (.json). It writes assets/teardown/menu.json and assets/teardown/loader.cfg into the build, leaving every other entry untouched.

The whole workflow

How to work it

Start to finish: drop a build in, describe the mods you want, and come out the other side with an APK on your headset. Every step names the exact button, and the end of this page lists what to do when a step refuses.

scanaskbindinjectbuildsign

The three parts

QuestForge is one file with three things in it, and they do different jobs.

PartWhat it is forOpen it with
Mod StudioReads your build, works out what is moddable, and assembles a menu from it.M
Teardown BenchYour workbench: search, disassemble, patch bytes, swap assets, rebuild and sign.B
The pathSix modules on the craft itself, if you want to understand what the studio is doing.C

Everything runs on your machine. Nothing is uploaded, and your progress is stored locally.

1 · Scan your build

Open Mod Studio and drop an APK on the scanner, or click it to browse. It walks every file in the build, indexes every identifier it finds, and scores them against the systems it knows.

What comes back:

  • Facts — engine, architecture, package, how much it read, how many symbols it indexed.
  • Detected systems — each with a confidence score and its evidence: how many references, which names, and which file they are strongest in.
Read the evidence, not just the percentage

A system backed by gravityModifier and GravityScale is a real finding. One backed only by bare type names is weak. The strongest hit usually sits in global-metadata.dat, which is where an il2cpp build keeps the game's own identifiers.

Never modded anything? Read this first

Nothing here assumes you know what any of it means. Five minutes and you will understand what the pieces are, which matters more than following steps you cannot debug.

What a mod menu actually is

A VR game on a headset is an Android app: a .apk file, which is a zip archive with the game inside it. Somewhere in there is the compiled game code, and a small library the app asks Android to load when it starts.

A mod menu is a second library that gets loaded alongside the game, draws a panel you can point at, and changes values in the running game when you press things. That is the whole idea. Everything else is detail.

The four pieces, and why each exists

PieceWhat it isWhy you need it
The buildThe game\u2019s .apkWhat you are modding. The studio reads it to find what the game can do.
The menuPictures and a table of touch areasWhat you see and press in the headset. Made here, injected into the .apk.
The runtimelibTEAR.so, compiled C++A picture cannot do anything. This is the part that runs inside the game.
The signatureA cryptographic stampAndroid refuses to install an app that is not signed. The bench does this for you.

Why there is a compiler step

The runtime has to be real ARM64 code, because that is what the headset\u2019s processor runs. A web page cannot produce that \u2014 no browser ships a compiler for another CPU. So the studio writes the project and you build it once with Android Studio\u2019s NDK. Once built, the same libTEAR.so works for every menu you make for that game. You only rebuild if the controls change.

What you need installed

ThingWhere fromWhat for
Android Studiodeveloper.android.comIt brings the next two.
NDK (Side by side)Tools → SDK Manager → SDK ToolsCompiles the runtime.
Platform-Toolssame placeGives you adb, for installing onto the headset.
Developer mode on the headsetMeta Quest phone appLets a PC install anything at all.

The shortest path that works

start to finish
1  drop the game\u2019s .apk on the scanner
2  ask for what you want      # "fly", "double my speed"
3  pick the button it opens with
4  Download libTEAR project   # once per game
5  run ndk-build              # once per game
6  Add built libTEAR.so
7  Inject mod menu
8  open it in the bench, Export APK   # signs it
9  adb install -r signed.apk

Steps 4 and 5 are the only ones that happen on a PC, and only the first time for a given game. If a step confuses you, Set it up for me in the studio walks through them one at a time and checks each one before moving on.

Three things that catch everyone

What happensWhat it means
\u201cINSTALL_PARSE_FAILED_NO_CERTIFICATES\u201dYou skipped the signing step. Export from the bench.
\u201cINSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE\u201dA different build is already installed. Uninstall it first.
Installs fine, menu never appearsNearly always the runtime: either it was not built, or an older one is in the build. The log tells you \u2014 see step 9.
Mod your own games, offline. Changing what other players can see or do in a live session is their game, not yours. Test in a private room or offline \u2014 it is also the only way to tell your bugs apart from a server rejecting the build.

2 · Say what you want

Type it in plain English. The studio shows the steps it is taking, then answers.

things you can say
# controls
fly
double my speed
low gravity
trigger fly, grip fly, fly speed
no cooldown on abilities
infinite health

# screens and pages
create a category called movement     # its own screen, with a row that opens it
double my speed                       # lands inside MOVEMENT
new page                              # a second page of MOVEMENT
back to the main menu                 # stop adding to it
god mode                              # back on the main menu
text saying tucker build v1
a disconnect button

# editing what is already there
set speed to 3
rename speed to Turbo
remove grip fly
clear

# widgets that are not controls
add a player preview
add a bar called health
add a readout showing fps
add an image slot called logo
add a divider

# the shape of the whole thing
make the whole menu a circle
make it a hexagon
make it a two column grid
make it a diamond
set sides to 8

# how the parts look
make the rows cards
make the toggles checkboxes
make the sliders dotted
make the menu cyan
make the background dark
make it wider and rounder
make it transparent
scanlines
no footer
monospace text
reset the panel

# or name any property outright
set width to 520
set glow to 0.6
set radius to 30
set columns to 3
set startAngle to 0
Why the preview can be trusted

The preview is not a mock-up of the menu \u2014 it is the menu. The same drawing pass makes the picture on this screen, the PNG that goes into the APK, and the table of touch regions beside it. A wheel\u2019s wedges become real wedges in the hit test, not the squares they sit in. So anything you can see here is what the headset shows, down to the pixel.

Several at once is fine — "fly, double speed and low gravity" is handled as three separate requests. The wording sets the value too: low gravity lands near 0.3×, double speed at 2×, max fly speed at the top of its range.

If there is no recipe for what you asked, the studio does not give up: it searches the symbols it indexed from your build and derives a control from the closest match, telling you which symbol it bound to.

Screens, not folders

A category is a screen of its own. The screen you are on shows a row with its name and how many things are inside; press it with your controller and the panel becomes that screen. Inside, a back row across the top returns you, and new page adds a page to that screen, with arrows at the bottom to walk between them. Categories inside categories nest as deep as you want.

Each screen-and-page becomes its own image in the APK, and the runtime swaps which one is on the quad when you press a row. There is no scrolling to design around and nothing to fold open — one press, one screen.

Say thisWhat it does
create a category called movementNew screen, plus the row that opens it
new pageAnother page of whichever screen you are filling
back to the main menuStop adding to the category
remove movementDrops the screen and everything on it

Sized for a headset, not a monitor

The defaults are drawn for VR: big rows, heavy separators, targets you can hit with a ray that is never quite still. The pre-flight does the arithmetic for you \u2014 it works out how many display pixels your smallest text ends up as, given how wide the panel is in metres and how far away it floats. Under about eleven and the lens smears it, so it tells you. Say bigger text, or set panelM to 0.6 to hang a wider panel.

3 · Pick the button that opens it

The studio will ask, and it will not build until you answer. Say "open with both grips", or tap a chip. The panel shows the bind in its own row, and it is written into loader.cfg as the real hotkey.

Why this is not optional

A menu with no open bind cannot be opened, no matter what else is right. This is the single most common reason a build comes back from the headset with nothing showing.

4 · Check the wiring

How to make it work lists every control with the approach it needs and the steps to get there.

TagMeans
PATCHA constant you can overwrite in place. Length-preserving, so nothing shifts.
HOOKBehaviour that has to be intercepted at runtime — a getter, a flag, a per-frame method.
CALLA method to invoke from a button.
UNBOUNDNothing in this build matched. The control ships disabled and marked not in build.

5 · Test run

Press Test run. The studio executes every control against a simulated game state and reports what actually moved:

a healthy test run
6 OF 6 DID SOMETHING
✓ Fly              useGravity: true → false
✓ Speed            velocity: 1 → 2
✓ Gravity          GravityScale: 1 → 0.3
✓ Ability cooldown CastTime: 1 → 0

A ! means the control runs but changes nothing — usually a multiplier still sitting at 1×. A ✕ means no binding at all.

What this proves and what it doesn't

It proves the logic is coherent and every control writes something. It cannot prove the offsets are right in your actual game — only the headset can tell you that.

6 · Read the pre-flight

Above the inject buttons is a checklist. Every row has to be sensible before the headset is worth putting on.

RowWhat it is checking
Build loadedAn APK is open.
N controlsHow many work, how many are inert.
Opens with…The bind is set.
Mod runtimeThe important one. Whether a native library exists that can read the menu at startup.
Sign it in the benchThe download is unsigned; the bench signs on export.

7 · Inject

Press Inject mod menu. Every original entry is copied through byte-for-byte — same compression, same CRC, never inflated — and these are added:

what lands in the APK
assets/teardown/menu.json       the menu, its ops and bindings
assets/teardown/menu.hit.json   each control's rectangle, 0..1
assets/teardown/menu_p0.png     the main screen, exactly as the preview draws it
assets/teardown/menu_p1.png     one image per screen and page
assets/teardown/loader.cfg      hotkey, runtime path, target package
assets/teardown/libTEAR.cpp     the runtime source

lib/arm64-v8a/libTEAR.so      the runtime you built
lib/arm64-v8a/libmain.so      the same runtime, under the name the game loads
lib/arm64-v8a/libmain_orig.so the game's own loader, moved aside and chained to

# the old signature is dropped (it is void after any edit)
# output is already 4-byte aligned, so you can skip zipalign
Why the renaming

Android never runs a native library just because it is in the APK. It runs one when Java asks for it by name. Unity asks for main, so the runtime goes in under that name and the stock loader is kept as libmain_orig.so; the runtime sets the menu up and then hands control straight back to it, so the game boots exactly as before. Put a library in lib/ and nothing else, and it simply never starts \u2014 which looks identical to a menu that does not work.

The menu looks right in the headset because the PNG is the preview. Nothing redraws your layout in C++, so nothing can drift.

8 · Build libTEAR.so

The studio cannot compile ARM64 in a browser, so it writes the project instead. Press Download libTEAR project, unzip it, and open a terminal in that folder — the one with jni inside it. There is nothing to fill in and nothing to cd to; the commands below find the NDK themselves.

On Windows, right-click empty space in the folder and choose Open in Terminal (Windows 10: Shift + right-click → Open PowerShell window here). That gives you PowerShell, which is the first block. %LOCALAPPDATA%-style variables do not expand in PowerShell, so the two Windows blocks are not interchangeable.

Windows — PowerShell (one line)
$n = @("$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Android\Sdk","$env:ANDROID_HOME","$env:ANDROID_SDK_ROOT","C:\Android\Sdk") | ForEach-Object { Get-ChildItem "$_\ndk" -Directory -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue } | Sort-Object Name -Descending | Select-Object -First 1; if ($n) { "Using NDK $($n.Name)"; & "$($n.FullName)\ndk-build.cmd" } else { "No NDK found - in Android Studio: Tools > SDK Manager > SDK Tools tab > tick NDK (Side by side) > Apply" }

It has to be one line. Paste a multi-line block into PowerShell and it stops at a >> prompt, waiting for a blank line — nothing runs and nothing is printed, which looks exactly like the command failing. If you are staring at a >> right now, press Enter once and it will run what you already pasted.

Windows — Command Prompt (cmd.exe)
set "NDK="
for /d %i in ("%LOCALAPPDATA%\Android\Sdk\ndk\*") do set "NDK=%i"
if not defined NDK (echo No NDK found - install it in Android Studio) else "%NDK%\ndk-build.cmd"
macOS / Linux
SDK="${ANDROID_HOME:-${ANDROID_SDK_ROOT:-$HOME/Android/Sdk}}"
NDK=$(ls -d "$SDK"/ndk/*/ 2>/dev/null | sort -V | tail -1)
if [ -z "$NDK" ]; then
  echo "No NDK found - install it in Android Studio > SDK Manager > SDK Tools"
else
  echo "Using $NDK"
  "$NDK/ndk-build"
fi

On macOS the SDK usually lives at ~/Library/Android/sdk instead — set SDK to that if the script reports nothing found.

what success looks like
[arm64-v8a] SharedLibrary  : libTEAR.so
[arm64-v8a] Install        : libTEAR.so => libs/arm64-v8a/libTEAR.so

# the file is now at, inside that same folder:
libs/arm64-v8a/libTEAR.so

# hand it back with "Add built libTEAR.so" and it is injected at:
lib/arm64-v8a/libTEAR.so

If you would rather be walked through it a step at a time — picking your OS and shell, checking the NDK is installed, then dropping the .so straight back in — use Guide me through it in the studio instead of this page.

Inside, libTEAR.cpp already contains the hit table, TEAR_HitTest(u, v) and TEAR_OnPress(index, amount) written out per control. What is left to you is drawing the quad, raycasting onto it, and your loader's symbol resolution.

9 · Sign it and put it on the headset

Open the built APK in Teardown Bench and use Export APK — it signs automatically. Then:

sideload
adb devices                        # headset listed?
adb install -r signed.apk

# if -r is refused, the signature differs from what's installed:
adb uninstall com.WaveX.MonkeySorcery
adb install signed.apk

adb logcat -s libTEAR             # did the runtime start?

Check this before anything else. Put the headset on, launch the game, and watch that last command. You should see:

a runtime that loaded
libTEAR: booting
libTEAR: init - game base 0x7xxxxxxxxx
libTEAR: menu: assets/teardown/menu.json
libTEAR: open bind: button_y
libTEAR: ready - MOD MENU, 8 items
libTEAR: chaining to libmain_orig.so

# then, once the engine is up and drawing:
libTEAR: libunity.so is up - patching its eglSwapBuffers import
libTEAR: hooked - expect a frame count below
libTEAR: first frame - we are on the render thread
libTEAR: compositor: ovrp_EnqueueSubmitLayer2        present
libTEAR: compositor: 8 of 8 entry points available
libTEAR: frame 600
libTEAR: frame 1200

The second block is the one that matters for getting a panel in front of you. first frame means this library is running inside the game’s render loop, once per presented frame, with the engine’s graphics context current — that is the only place a panel can be drawn from. The compositor: lines report which of the headset’s own layer entry points are reachable from inside the process; those are what put a quad in the world without touching the game’s own rendering.

Those six lines mean the library loaded, read your menu and handed the engine back. No libTEAR lines at all means it never started \u2014 check that lib/arm64-v8a/libmain.so in the installed APK is your file and not the stock one. A line saying no libmain_orig.so to chain to means the rename did not happen: re-inject from an untouched copy of the game.

When it refuses

SymptomCauseFix
Menu never appearsNo runtime in the buildPre-flight will say so. Build libTEAR.so, or put back the mod menu that was stripped.
Menu never appears, runtime is thereNo open bind, or the wrong oneSet it in the studio; check hotkey in loader.cfg.
INSTALL_PARSE_FAILED_NO_CERTIFICATESUnsignedExport from the bench, or run apksigner.
INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLEDifferent signing key to what is installedUninstall first, then install.
Installs, then crashes instantlyA library the game needs is missing, or a patch broke somethingInstall the untouched build first to prove the chain, then add one change at a time.
Control does nothing in gameOffset was a string hit, not the real fieldConfirm it in the bench — search the value, disassemble around the address.
Control shows greyed outNothing in the build matched itExpected. Bind it by hand in menu.json, or drop it.

What it can't do

  • Compile. No compiler exists in a browser — hence the NDK project.
  • Sign. No key lives here; the bench holds that.
  • Guarantee an offset. Addresses come from scanning strings. They are a strong starting point, not proof. The bench is where you confirm one.
